## The question

Every permitted waste site in England reports the waste it receives, and the Environment
Agency publishes the results. Each site is listed under an operator name, but large
companies run dozens of sites through separate legal entities. Veolia, for example,
appears under many different company names in the data.

Once operators are linked to legal entities and parent groups:

- How concentrated is waste handling in England?
- Which groups own the capacity?

## Data

| Source | What it provides | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| EA Waste Data Interrogator 2025, "Wastes received" (Version 2) | 365,819 rows covering 6,307 permits and 3,782 operator names; 260.1M tonnes received | One row per site, waste type and origin |
| EA Waste Data Interrogator 2025, "Wastes removed" (Version 2) | 134,811 rows covering 6,030 permits; 114.3M tonnes removed | Not used for the headline figures; planned for a later look at flows |
| Companies House free company data | Registered names, company numbers, status, addresses | TODO: snapshot date; live companies only |

This is my own analysis. The Environment Agency and Companies House have not reviewed or endorsed it, and the classifications and matches are mine and may contain errors.

I checked the loaded data against the Environment Agency's own report in the workbook. For the removed-waste file, the total (114,259,980 tonnes) and the totals by waste chapter, fate and destination match exactly. The same holds for the received file.

The permit number (EPR number) identifies a site reliably. The operator field is free text,
and it is the thing this project links to legal entities.

### What "tonnes received" does and doesn't mean

Waste often passes through several sites: a transfer station receives it, and a treatment
plant receives it from the transfer station. Each site reports it as received, so the
figures measure throughput at sites, not how much waste England produces. Because of this
I never add "received" and "removed" together, and I describe the measure as tonnes
received throughout.

## Scope

I use all permitted sites in England for 2025, but exclude EWC chapter 19 ("waste and
water treatment wastes") from the headline analysis. It is 100.9M of the 260.1M tonnes,
and two sub-chapters explain most of it:

- **Wastewater treatment plants: 52.6M tonnes from only 133 operators.** This is mainly
  water company sewage sludge. Thames Water alone accounts for 32M tonnes in this chapter.
- **Mechanical treatment of waste: 28.3M tonnes from 934 operators.** This is the output
  of sorting and treatment sites, which is received again at the next site it goes to.

Leaving it out leaves about 159M tonnes of mostly primary waste (construction and
demolition, municipal, and commercial streams) received by 3,683 operators. Chapter 19 is
reported separately at the end.

::: {#scope .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import duckdb

f = "'data/interim/waste_received_2025.parquet'"
operators = duckdb.sql(f"""
    SELECT operator, COUNT(DISTINCT epr_number) AS permits,
           ROUND(SUM(tonnes_received)) AS tonnes_received
    FROM {f}
    WHERE ewc_chapter NOT LIKE '19%'
    GROUP BY operator
""").df()
```
:::


## Cleaning and standardising names

Within the EA data the operator names are already consistent: no permit appears under more
than one spelling, and standardising removes only two duplicates among 3,782 names. So the
work is in linking to Companies House, not in tidying the EA names.

I standardise names (lower case, punctuation removed, `&` read as "and", leading "The"
dropped) and split off the legal form (Limited, Ltd, PLC, LLP and so on). The legal form is
kept as a separate field because two companies can share a stem and still be different
legal entities. The same function is applied to Companies House names.

| EA operator name | Stem | Legal form |
|---|---|---|
| VEOLIA ES (UK) LIMITED | veolia es uk | limited |
| Alchemy Metals Limited t/a Waste Mission | alchemy metals | limited |
| LONGWATER (GRAVEL) COMPANY LIMITED (THE) | longwater gravel company | limited |

::: {#clean .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from waste_operators.clean import split_legal_form, classify_operator

operators[["stem", "legal_form"]] = operators["operator"].apply(
    lambda n: pd.Series(split_legal_form(n))
)
operators["kind"] = operators["operator"].apply(classify_operator)
```
:::


### Operators that are not companies

About 740 of the 3,683 operators have no legal form. Sorting them roughly by name:

| Group | Operators | Tonnes received |
|---|---|---|
| Public bodies (mostly councils and NHS trusts) | about 129 | about 5.0M |
| Individuals or unregistered businesses | about 583 | about 4.2M |
| Unclear (for example skip hire firms with no suffix) | 31 | about 0.6M |

These are rule-based groupings, not hand-checked. TODO: hand-check the unclear group and
a sample of the others. Together they hold about 6% of the in-scope tonnage, so about 94%

## Limitations

- **Throughput, not generation.** Tonnes received counts waste each time a site receives it.
- **Rule-based classification.** The split between companies, public bodies and individuals
  is heuristic.
- **Live companies only.** The Companies House free file lists live companies, so operators
  that have since been dissolved or renamed may not match.
- **One year.** This covers 2025 only.
- **Permitted sites only.** The data covers permitted waste facilities in England and excludes exempt facilities.
